doc.title: Denny Zeitlin interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Standards versus originals on records
summary: Producers like John Hammond wanted recognizable tunes plus originals; Zeitlin prefers mixing the two so listeners have a foothold.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: When you do a recording, in the old days an LP and now CDs, the people you’re working with, either producers or record companies, do they like to see well-known tunes on the recordings as well as your own material?

I think that’s varied over the years, Monk. Like when I first started recording for Columbia back in the early ‘60s, John Hammond, who was my producer, liked very much the idea of recognizable tunes plus originals. And that’s not an unusual stance for a producer to take. But over the years I’ve had projects where I’ve done albums totally of original compositions and albums all of standards, and I think it really depends on the record label, what their predilection is at the moment. I generally like to do mixtures because I think it’s interesting to share with the listener what a musician does with a well- known tune in terms of how you might re-harmonize it or arrange it, and how you will work the changes of something they’re familiar with. They have a place to stand to listen to the music. So sometimes it helps them get a foot in the door. An original composition offers the musician total carte blanche of the territory he wants to cover and that freedom
is wonderful but sometimes it’s a little harder for the listener to get into. So having an album that has a balance of the two often I think is the best way to go.
